title: Branch Office vs Liaison Office Registration in Nepal
content:
For many overseas companies, the first practical question about operating in Nepal is a simple one: how do we establish a presence here? Two structures are available, and the choice matters, because the tax and immigration authorities treat them very differently. A branch office can trade, sign contracts and invoice in Nepal. A liaison office cannot. It exists to study the market and coordinate, and it must be funded from abroad.

Choose the wrong one and you either breach the terms of your approval or take on tax and reporting duties you did not need. This guide explains the difference, who qualifies, the documents, the process and the ongoing obligations, so the decision is an informed one.

Quick answer

A foreign company that wants a physical presence in Nepal has two routes. A branch office trades, contracts and invoices. A liaison office is non-trading and limited to market research and coordination. Both require prior approval from the Department of Industry (DOI), after which the office is registered with the Office of the Company Registrar (OCR) under the Companies Act, 2063. A branch office is for doing business in Nepal; a liaison office is for studying it.

Which law applies?

A foreign company establishing a place of business in Nepal must register with the OCR. Section 154 of the Companies Act, 2063 requires registration within one month of establishing that place of business. Two regimes apply depending on the activity.

A branch office is registered under Section 155 for trading activity.

A liaison office is registered under Section 156 for non-trading activity such as market study and coordination.

In both cases, approval from the DOI must be obtained first, and foreign exchange and repatriation are supervised by Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB).

Branch office versus liaison office

Feature Branch office Liaison office
Permitted activities Trade, contract, invoice, import and export for the parent Market research, coordination and liaison only
Can earn income in Nepal Yes No, and it must be funded by the parent
Tax registration PAN and VAT as applicable Limited, not for trading income
Profit repatriation Yes, after tax clearance and NRB compliance Not applicable
Renewal Periodic renewal required Periodic renewal required
Typical use Executing contracts and projects, sales Feasibility study and market entry research

A branch office is an extension of the foreign parent. It does not have a separate legal personality, which means the parent remains responsible for the branch's obligations. That is an important point for risk planning.

Who should choose a branch office?

A branch office suits a foreign company that already has business in Nepal, whether executing a contract, servicing clients or running a project. If the Nepal operation needs to sign agreements in its own name, issue invoices, or move goods across the border, the branch is the right vehicle. Because it is tax-registered, income earned here is taxed here, and profits can be repatriated after tax clearance and NRB approval.

Who should choose a liaison office?

A liaison office is for a foreign company that is not yet doing business in Nepal and only wants to study the market, gather information or coordinate with partners. It may not earn income here, may not invoice, and is funded through remittances from the parent. It is a low-commitment way to establish a presence before committing to a branch or a locally incorporated subsidiary.

Eligibility and the negative list

Foreign companies in most sectors can apply for branch or liaison approval, but Nepal maintains a negative list of activities reserved for Nepali citizens. These include certain trading activities, travel and trekking, and some cottage industries. Activity on the negative list cannot be approved for a branch or liaison office, and sector eligibility is assessed at the DOI stage.

Documents commonly required

  • An application to the DOI with the proposed office details
  • Certificate of incorporation of the parent, apostilled or consularised
  • Memorandum and articles of association, or equivalent charter, of the parent
  • A board resolution authorising the Nepal office and nominating a representative
  • Audited financial statements of the parent for the last few years
  • Passport copy of the authorised representative
  • A power of attorney in favour of a local representative
  • A commitment to fund the office, for liaison offices
  • The underlying contract, licence or project document, for branch offices

Documents executed abroad generally need notarisation and apostille or consular legalisation, and non-English documents need certified translation.

The process, step by step

  1. Prepare and legalise documents in the parent's home country.
  2. File the application with the DOI, including the activity details and source of funds.
  3. Obtain DOI approval to establish a branch or liaison office.
  4. Reserve the office name at the OCR.
  5. Register with the OCR under the relevant section of the Companies Act within the statutory period.
  6. Complete tax registration, obtaining a PAN and, for a branch, VAT where applicable.
  7. Open a bank account and complete NRB reporting for the initial remittance.
  8. Register with the local ward and obtain any sector-specific licence, such as one from the Nepal Tourism Board.

A worked example

A European engineering firm wins a maintenance contract in Nepal and needs a local presence to invoice the client. It chooses a branch office, because the operation must contract and bill locally. A second firm, still evaluating whether the Nepali market is worth entering, registers a liaison office instead, keeping its costs low and its options open while it studies demand. If the first firm had registered a liaison office, it could not have invoiced, and the contract would have stalled. If the second had registered a branch, it would have taken on tax and reporting obligations for an operation that earns nothing.

Cost and timeline

Approval and registration fees are modest by regional standards, but the realistic timeline depends on document readiness. Expect roughly two to six weeks for DOI approval and OCR registration once the file is complete, with foreign exchange and tax steps adding one to two weeks. Documents legalised abroad are usually the biggest source of delay.

Ongoing compliance

Both structures must renew their registration periodically and keep the OCR informed of changes to the registered office or representative. A branch office has full tax filing obligations, must maintain proper accounts, and must route profits through tax clearance for repatriation. A liaison office must avoid anything that looks like trading, with no invoices and no local income, and must document that it is funded by the parent.

Common mistakes

  • Registering a liaison office, then trading through it. This breaches the terms of approval and risks cancellation.
  • Missing the one-month registration window after establishing a place of business.
  • Skipping legalisation or apostille of foreign documents, which causes rejection.
  • Ignoring NRB reporting on the initial capital or funding remittance.
  • Assuming a branch is a subsidiary. It is not, and the parent carries the liability.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a foreign company have to register in Nepal? Registration with the OCR is required within one month of establishing a place of business in Nepal.

Can a liaison office earn income in Nepal? No. A liaison office is non-trading and must be funded by the parent through remittances.

Can a branch office repatriate profits? Yes, after paying applicable taxes in Nepal and completing NRB compliance.

Does a branch office have a separate legal personality? No. A branch is an extension of the foreign parent, which remains liable for its obligations.

Is DOI approval needed before OCR registration? Yes. A foreign company must obtain DOI approval before registering the branch or liaison office with the OCR.

Can a foreign company open a branch in a restricted sector? No. Activities on Nepal's negative list are reserved and cannot be approved for branch or liaison registration.

How long is the approval valid? Approvals are time-bound and must be renewed periodically, and the renewal cycle is stated in the approval.

title: Indian Investors Registering a Company in Nepal: 2026 Guide
content:
Indian businesses have long been among the most active investors in Nepal, and for good reason. The border is open, trade ties run deep, and the tax treaty between the two countries reduces the cost of moving money across it. The legal pathway, though, is the same one every foreign investor follows, and that is where most Indian founders are surprised: there is no special route, only familiar ones made easier by geography.

This guide explains how an Indian investor registers a company in Nepal, what is genuinely different, and where the practical traps lie.

Quick answer

Indian investors register a company in Nepal under the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act (FITTA), 2075 (2019) and the Companies Act, 2063, on the same footing as other foreign investors. Nepal generally permits up to 100% foreign ownership in sectors that are not on the negative list. The process runs through the Department of Industry (DOI) or Investment Board Nepal (IBN), the Office of the Company Registrar (OCR), and Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB). What differs for Indian investors is mostly practical: cross-border documentation, currency and banking treatment, and the relief available under the India-Nepal tax treaty.

Is Indian investment treated differently?

Indian investors are foreign investors under FITTA. The framework is identical: the minimum investment, the sector eligibility, the approval authority and the repatriation rules apply the same way to an investor from Delhi as to one from Dubai.

What Indian investors gain is convenience. The open border and Indian rupee convertibility make funding simpler than for investors from further afield. The India-Nepal Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) can reduce withholding on certain cross-border payments. None of this removes the formal requirements. Capital still has to be brought in through banking channels and recorded at NRB, and the investment still needs approval.

The legal framework

  • Companies Act, 2063 (2006) governs incorporation and governance.
  • FITTA, 2075 (2019) governs foreign investment approval and repatriation.
  • Industrial Enterprises Act, 2076 (2020) classifies industries and sets out incentives.
  • Nepal Rastra Bank rules govern foreign exchange, capital inflow and remittance.
  • The India-Nepal DTAA provides relief from double taxation on cross-border income.

Ownership and the negative list

Most sectors allow full foreign ownership, and an Indian company can often hold 100% of a Nepali subsidiary. The exception is the negative list, which reserves certain activities for Nepali citizens. It covers areas such as parts of retail trading, cottage and small industries, travel and trekking agencies, and certain services. Sector eligibility is confirmed at the approval stage, so it is worth checking before you commit to a structure. A joint venture that assumes 100% ownership of a restricted activity will not be approved.

Minimum investment

FITTA sets a general minimum investment per foreign investor, and the figure applies per investor. In a joint venture, each foreign shareholder must meet it separately. Because the threshold is set in Nepali rupees and has been adjusted over time, confirm the current amount with the DOI or a licensed practitioner before you commit capital.

The process, step by step

  1. Confirm sector eligibility against the negative list.
  2. Reserve the company name at the OCR.
  3. Apply for foreign investment approval to the DOI, or IBN above the applicable project-size threshold.
  4. Incorporate the company at the OCR, filing the memorandum and articles with the approved investment details.
  5. Register for PAN and VAT at the Inland Revenue Department, and register with the local ward.
  6. Open a bank account and bring the approved capital in through banking channels.
  7. Complete NRB reporting confirming the capital inflow, and any technology transfer.
  8. Obtain sector licences where required, such as tourism or education.

A worked example

An Indian manufacturer wants a wholly owned subsidiary in Nepal to serve the local market. Because manufacturing is open to foreign investment, the route is straightforward. The company's board passes a resolution authorising the investment, the Indian incorporation documents are notarised and apostilled, and the file goes to the DOI for approval. Once approved, the subsidiary is incorporated, capital is remitted from India through banking channels, and NRB records the inflow. The DTAA shapes how dividends are taxed on the way back. The whole sequence takes weeks, not months, provided the Indian paperwork is ready before filings begin.

Documents commonly required

  • Passport or corporate registration documents of the Indian investor
  • Certificate of incorporation and board resolution for a corporate investor
  • Memorandum and articles of association of the parent, where applicable
  • Source-of-funds declaration and project report
  • Proof of registered office address in Nepal, with the owner's consent
  • Director and shareholder consent letters
  • Notarised, apostilled and translated documents where executed in India

Tax and repatriation

A company incorporated in Nepal is a Nepali tax resident and is taxed on the income it earns here. Dividends paid to the Indian parent may attract withholding tax, and the DTAA can affect that. Profits and dividends can be repatriated after tax clearance and NRB approval. Indian investors should also consider how the home country will tax the Nepali income, and claim foreign tax credit under the treaty where it applies, so the same income is not taxed twice.

How long it takes

Expect roughly two to six weeks for approval and incorporation once documents are ready, with tax, banking and NRB steps adding one to two weeks. Cross-border legalisation and sector approvals are the usual sources of delay.

Where Indian investors go wrong

Assuming Indian investors are exempt. They are not. FITTA approval is required.

Ignoring the negative list. Planning a structure that cannot be approved wastes the filing cost and months of time.

Bringing funds informally. Capital must be documented through banking channels with NRB recording, or the investment is defective.

Missing the per-investor minimum in a joint venture.

Overlooking the DTAA and paying withholding that could have been reduced or eliminated.

Frequently asked questions

Can an Indian citizen own 100% of a Nepali company? In sectors not on the negative list, yes. Up to 100% foreign ownership is generally permitted.

Does Indian investment need DOI approval? Yes. Indian investors are foreign investors under FITTA 2019 and require approval.

Is the minimum investment lower for Indian investors? The general threshold applies to foreign investors. Confirm the current figure, as it is set in Nepali rupees and can change.

Can an Indian company open a branch in Nepal instead? Yes. A foreign company, including an Indian one, may register a branch or liaison office, subject to DOI approval and OCR registration.

Can profits be sent back to India? Yes, after tax clearance, NRB approval and, where relevant, applying the DTAA.

How long does it take? Typically two to six weeks for approval and incorporation once the file is complete.

The resource is real, the demand is growing, and the country has spent years building the framework to bring projects like these to life. What surprises most developers is not that the process is rigorous, but that it is sequential. Each gate must be passed before the next one opens, and a project that tries to move ahead of its paperwork stalls in ways that are expensive to reverse.

This guide walks through that sequence in plain terms, so you can plan around it rather than be surprised by it.

I. The Three-Gate Approval Model: How Nepal's Hydropower Registration Actually Works Reference Level

Based on Pluto Associates's experience handling hydropower licensing applications since 2018, Nepal's hydropower registration is best understood as a Three-Gate Approval Model, three sequential eligibility tests that must each be passed before the next phase is meaningful. Developers who treat registration as a single linear process typically discover the three-gate structure only when they encounter the second or third gate unexpectedly late.

Gate 1, Eligibility

Can You Apply at All?

  • Is the river stretch available in DOED's inventory? [15]
  • Is the site outside protected area legal uncertainty? (2024 ruling)
  • Is the capacity below the IBN threshold (200 MW / NPR 6B)?
  • Does the developer meet DOED's financial credibility standard?
Gate 2, Technical

Can the Project Be Approved?

  • Survey license → feasibility studies → hydrological data
  • IEE or EIA depending on size and location [4]
  • Forest land clearance from Ministry of Forests
  • Grid connectivity agreement with NEA [14]
  • Generation license application to DOED or IBN [1]
Gate 3, Commercial

Can the Project Be Financed?

  • PPA negotiation and signing with NEA [14]
  • FDI approval and NRB capital recording [5]
  • Construction financing closure with lenders
  • Community and public equity tranches (if applicable)
  • Construction → COD → tax holiday activation
Why the Three-Gate Model Matters Most registration timelines fail because developers treat all three gates as one sequential queue. Gate 1 can be confirmed in days. Gate 2 takes 3-8 years. Gate 3 can run in parallel with late-stage Gate 2 activities. The forest clearance application, the most documented bottleneck in Gate 2, must be filed in Month 3 of the survey period, not after Gate 2 closes. This single scheduling decision is the largest controllable variable in Nepal hydropower development timelines.

II. Legal Framework: Six Statutes, One Project Reference Level

III. The Survey License (Adhyayan Anumati Patra) Verify Availability First

Entity Definition, Survey License

A Survey License (Adhyayan Anumati Patra) is a preliminary permit issued by Nepal's Department of Electricity Development (DOED) granting a developer exclusive rights to conduct feasibility studies, hydrological assessments, and environmental baseline surveys on a designated river stretch for a period of up to 5 years. [1] It does not authorize construction, water diversion, or any permanent infrastructure.

Survey licenses are issued on a first-come, first-served basis from DOED's national river inventory, a register of all river stretches and their current license status. [15] Before any application preparation, developers must confirm the target stretch is unlicensed, not reserved for government projects, and not within a protected area zone made legally uncertain by the 2024 Constitutional Bench ruling.

Trap #1
0
Before All

Confirm River Stretch Availability, Before Any Preparation Cost

Applications for stretches already under license, reserved by government, or inside a protected area boundary are rejected, after all preparation costs have been incurred. DOED does not refund application fees or preparation costs on rejected applications. This confirmation costs very little and prevents the most avoidable expense in Nepal hydropower registration. Zero refund on rejected applications, do this step before any professional engagement

Survey License Application to DOED

Submit detailed topographic maps (minimum scale 1:25,000), preliminary cost estimates with methodology, developer financial credibility certificate (from home-country bank, dated within 6 months), proof of technical capacity, and a proposed study work program. For foreign developers: company incorporation documents (apostilled), board resolution authorizing Nepal investment, and passport copies of all named investors. [15]

What Must Be Completed During the Survey Period

Detailed feasibility study confirming generation potential and technical approach; hydrological gauge data over minimum 1-2 complete seasons; grid connectivity study with NEA confirming evacuation pathway; [14] environmental baseline assessment establishing IEE or EIA requirement; and community social baseline survey where required by EIA terms of reference.

Start forest clearance application in Month 3, not after generation license

IV. The Generation License (Utpadan Anumati Patra) Legal Confirmation Required

Frequently Asked Questions

How do you register a hydropower project in Nepal?
Hydropower registration requires two licenses: a Survey License (Adhyayan Anumati Patra) from DOED for up to 5 years to study a river stretch, then a Generation License (Utpadan Anumati Patra) for 30-35 years to build and operate. Projects above 200 MW or NPR 6 billion go to IBN. Foreign investors need FDI approval under FITTA 2019. A PPA with NEA is required before construction financing closes.
The process spans the Three-Gate Approval Model: Gate 1 confirms eligibility (river availability, protected area status, threshold routing); Gate 2 delivers the technical approvals (feasibility, environmental clearance, generation license); Gate 3 closes commercial viability (PPA, financing, COD). Statutory timelines suggest 3-5 years total. An empirical study of 34 projects found actual median timelines of 5-12 years. [12] Financial models should use the empirical range, not the statutory estimate.
Can foreigners own 100% of a Nepal hydropower project?
Yes. FITTA 2019 permits up to 100% foreign equity in hydropower generation companies. Hydropower is not on FITTA's negative list. The minimum FDI threshold of NPR 20 million applies to the foreign investor's contribution. Projects below NPR 6 billion go to DoI for FDI approval; larger projects go to IBN.
Market practice has added community and public equity conventions not required by law. [5] A 10% tranche to project-affected communities and a 10% NEPSE IPO appear in many Nepal hydropower projects, not because FITTA mandates them, but because community cooperation on land access and EIA consultations is practically essential for project viability in many locations. Whether this applies to a specific project requires site-specific assessment, not general guidance.
What tax incentives does Nepal offer for hydropower projects?
100% income tax exemption for 10 years from COD; 50% reduction for years 11-15; 1% concessional customs duty on machinery; full VAT exemption on generation equipment; 12-year loss carry-forward under FITTA 2019.
The single most important detail: the holiday starts from Commercial Operation Date (COD), not from generation license issuance. [5] Given the 15-month median COD slippage observed in practice, [12] most projects lose a meaningful portion of their tax holiday to RCOD delays. COD definition must be identical in the generation license and PPA, a one-sided definition has historically been resolved in NEA's favor in disputed cases.
What environmental approval is required for hydropower in Nepal?
Projects below ~50 MW require an IEE. Projects above ~50 MW, near protected areas, or requiring significant land acquisition require a full EIA with public consultations. The 2024 Constitutional Bench ruling creates site-specific legal uncertainty for projects adjacent to national parks and conservation areas.
Forest land clearance, a separate process from the IEE/EIA, is the single most documented cause of construction delay in Nepal hydropower, with actual median timelines of 12-24 months against a statutory expectation of 6-12 months. [12] The forest clearance application must be initiated in Month 3 of the survey period, not after the generation license is issued. Sites near protected area boundaries additionally require a current written legal opinion on the 2024 ruling's effect, no general guidance, including this article, substitutes for that site-specific analysis.
What is the PPA tariff for hydropower in Nepal?
For run-of-river projects up to ~25 MW: ERC fixed rates of approximately NPR 4.80/unit (wet season) and NPR 8.40/unit (dry season) with 3-5% annual escalation for 8 years. Projects above ~25 MW negotiate bilateral tariffs with NEA.
The wet/dry tariff asymmetry reflects Nepal's monsoon hydrology, run-of-river plants generate 60-70% more power during the June, November wet season than during the dry winter months. [14] This seasonality is the central financial planning challenge for Nepal hydropower: dry-season debt service coverage ratios, not annual averages, are the critical lender constraint. ERC rates cited here are current as of June 2026 and should be confirmed with ERC or NEA before financial modeling, as schedules are revised periodically.

title: FDI Registration Process in Nepal: Complete Step-by-Step Guide (2026)
content:
Foreign investors often describe the same experience: they know Nepal is open for business, they have a project in mind, and yet the registration process feels like a maze with too many doors. This guide walks through the whole route in plain language, from the first approval to the day your capital is recorded at the central bank, so you can plan with realistic expectations rather than guesswork.

If you would rather have a lawyer run the sequence for you, that is what we do every week. If you want to understand it yourself first, keep reading.

Quick answer: how does FDI registration work in Nepal?

Foreign direct investment in Nepal is registered through five core stages. You obtain industry approval from the Department of Industry (DOI), or from Investment Board Nepal (IBN) for very large projects. You incorporate the company at the Office of the Company Registrar (OCR). You complete tax and local registration. You register the industry at the DOI. Finally, you bring the money in through Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB). The full journey usually takes three to five months, and the legal minimum investment is NPR 20 million (roughly USD 150,000) under the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act, 2075 (FITTA).

Key fact Detail
Governing law FITTA 2075 (2019); Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Regulations, 2077; Companies Act 2063
Minimum investment NPR 20 million per foreign investor
Approval authority Department of Industry (DOI), or Investment Board Nepal (IBN) for projects above NPR 4 billion
Capital regulator Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB)
Typical timeline Three to five months end to end
Investment routes Equity investment, loan investment, re-investment of profits

In our practice, most delays come not from the law but from two avoidable places: incomplete documentation at the DOI stage, and banking friction at the NRB stage. Both are manageable when preparation starts early.

What counts as foreign direct investment in Nepal?

Under FITTA, foreign direct investment is money a foreign investor puts into Nepal through one of three routes.

Equity investment. The foreign investor subscribes to shares of a Nepali company. This may be a wholly owned subsidiary or a joint venture with local partners. Most of our clients take this route.

Loan investment. The foreign investor lends to the Nepali company, usually alongside equity. This is common in projects with heavy upfront cost, such as hotels and hydropower, where loan finance smooths the cash flow until revenue begins.

Re-investment. Profits earned in Nepal are put back into the same business or another qualifying industry rather than taken out. This keeps capital working locally and can support expansion without a fresh inbound remittance.

FITTA also covers technology transfer agreements, including licensing, management contracts and franchise know-how, which can be registered alongside an equity investment.

Who qualifies as a foreign investor?

The definition is wide. It covers foreign citizens, foreign companies, firms and organisations. It includes Non-Resident Nepalis holding NRN citizenship or an NRN card under the relevant rules. Indian nationals and Indian companies follow the same FITTA pathway as everyone else; the India-Nepal trade and transit arrangements affect the banking logistics, not the approval route itself.

Where foreign investment is restricted

Nepal maintains a negative list, which bars foreign investment in certain activities. It includes primary agriculture, real estate outside specified construction development, retail business below certain thresholds, internal courier services, local catering, money changing and remittance services, and travel and guide services, among others.

The list is not static. It shifts with each Finance Act, so we verify the current position against the latest law before any filing. If you have a sector in mind and you are not sure whether it is open, that is usually the first question worth answering. It is far cheaper to check than to discover the conflict after you have incorporated a company around the wrong activity.

The FDI registration process, step by step

This is the sequence we follow for a typical wholly owned subsidiary. Each step builds on the last, so the order matters.

Step 1: Name reservation and preliminary structuring

Before anyone approaches the DOI, we reserve the proposed company name at the OCR and settle three things: the shareholding structure, the scope of the industry, and the registered address. This stage is short but important. The DOI approves your project, the OCR registers your company, and the two documents have to describe the same business. Getting the industry classification right now prevents rework later.

Timeline: two to three days for name clearance.

Step 2: Application for foreign investment approval

The application is filed online through the DOI system, or with IBN for large projects. The file typically includes a project report covering market, technical and financial aspects with a funding plan and implementation schedule, passport and bio-data of the investor and directors, the investing entity's incorporation documents (apostilled or notarised, and translated where needed), a board resolution authorising the Nepal investment, a financial credibility letter from the investor's bank, a power of attorney appointing a Nepal-based representative, and, where relevant, a joint venture agreement.

Timeline: one to two weeks for screening. The approval certificate issues once the DOI is satisfied the project meets FITTA criteria.

Step 3: Company incorporation at the OCR

With the FDI approval in hand, the company is incorporated under the Companies Act, 2063. You file the memorandum and articles of association in the prescribed format, pay registration fees calculated on authorised capital, and receive the certificate of incorporation.

Timeline: about one week after a complete filing.

Step 4: Tax and local registration

The company obtains a Permanent Account Number from the Inland Revenue Department, registers for VAT where turnover thresholds apply, then registers with the local ward office and obtains a recommendation from the local level.

Timeline: about one week combined.

Step 5: Industry registration at the DOI

The company then registers the industry itself at the DOI, classified as small, medium or large scale depending on fixed capital. This step is what unlocks later benefits, including tax incentives and repatriation facilities tied to the approved project.

Timeline: one to two weeks.

Step 6: Non-blacklisting certificate

A non-blacklisted certificate from the Credit Information Bureau confirms that neither the investor nor the company carries a history of defaulted loans. Banks will ask for it at the capital injection stage, so it is worth obtaining in good time.

Step 7: NRB approval and capital injection

This is the step investors most often underestimate. To bring funds in, you open a corporate bank account, apply through the commercial bank to NRB for approval to remit the investment, remit the money through formal banking channels with the purpose stated as share or loan investment, and obtain the NRB remittance record.

That record matters more than people realise. It is the proof that your capital entered Nepal lawfully, and it is what allows you to repatriate profits and sale proceeds years later. Every rupee of capital should enter through banking channels with correct documentation. Investors who skip proper NRB recording frequently run into serious obstacles when they eventually want to take money out.

Timeline: two to four weeks depending on the bank.

Step 8: Post-registration compliance

After capital injection, the company settles into ongoing compliance: annual general meetings and OCR filings, tax returns, industry renewal where applicable, social security fund registration for employees, and sector-specific licences such as tourism, IT-enabled services or manufacturing standards.

How long the process really takes

Stage Realistic duration
Name clearance and structuring Three to five days
DOI or IBN FDI approval Two to six weeks
Company incorporation One week
PAN, VAT and ward registration One week
Industry registration One to two weeks
NRB approval and capital injection Two to four weeks
Total Three to five months

These timelines assume complete documentation. Apostille or consular legalisation of home-country corporate documents frequently adds two to four weeks if it is not started early, which is why we begin that paperwork in parallel with everything else.

What it costs

Government fees depend on authorised capital and industry scale, and the registration fee slabs under the Companies Act and DOI schedules change with each Finance Act. Beyond government fees, budget for document apostille and notarisation, certified translations, and professional fees. We provide a written fee estimate once we have reviewed the project structure, so you can see the full picture before committing.

Where FDI applications get stuck

From files we have reviewed and remediated, the same problems recur.

A weak project report. Thin market sizing, unrealistic financial projections, or a mismatch between the declared scope and the actual activity will stall approval.

Credibility gaps. Bank letters that do not meet the DOI's expectations on format or recency are a common and avoidable hold-up.

A negative-list conflict. Proposing an activity that falls within the restricted list without realising it wastes months.

Structure mismatches. Shareholding recorded in the memorandum that does not match the FDI approval creates problems at incorporation and later at banking.

Banking channel errors. Remitting funds before NRB recording, or through informal channels, puts your future repatriation rights at risk. This is the single most expensive mistake we see.

Frequently asked questions

What is the minimum FDI amount in Nepal? NPR 20 million per foreign investor under FITTA 2075. This applies to equity investment, and the amount must come in through formal banking channels.

Can a foreigner own 100% of a company in Nepal? Yes, in most sectors. FITTA permits wholly foreign-owned companies, except in sectors on the negative list or where specific laws require local participation.

How long does the FDI process take? Realistically three to five months from name clearance to recorded capital injection, assuming the documents are ready when filings begin.

Do Indian investors follow a different process? No separate approval track exists. Indian investors use the same DOI or IBN route. The practical differences show up in banking documentation under the India-Nepal treaty arrangements.

Can profits be repatriated out of Nepal? Yes. FITTA guarantees repatriation of profits, dividends and sale proceeds, provided the original investment was properly recorded with NRB. This is exactly why the NRB discipline in Step 7 matters so much.

Is physical presence in Nepal required? Not for the registration stages. A power of attorney lets a Nepal-based lawyer file on your behalf. In most cases, directors will need visit visas for banking formalities and operations.

What happens if my sector is on the negative list? It cannot be approved for full foreign ownership. Sometimes the activity can be restructured to fall outside the restricted category, or handled through a different structure. This is worth checking before you commit capital.

How much capital must I bring in at once? The approved investment is not always required in a single transfer. Depending on the approval and the project, capital can be brought in stages, and we map that schedule during structuring.

How Pluto Associates can help

We have guided foreign investors through Nepal's FDI regime since 2019, from DOI approval through incorporation, NRB capital recording and annual compliance. Our team works in English and Nepali, provides fixed-scope fee proposals, and gives you a single point of contact from first consultation to first dividend.

If you would like a clear view of how this applies to your own project, contact our team for a consultation, message us on WhatsApp, or call +977 9802356987. We will tell you what is possible, what it costs, and how long it takes.

title: How Foreign Investors Can Set Up a Company in Nepal in 2025
content:
Foreign investors looking at Nepal tend to ask the same question in the same tone of mild caution: is it actually workable, and how long until we can trade? The reassuring answer is that the framework is well established, and the sequence is clear. The caution is worth keeping, because the order of the steps matters. Approval comes before incorporation, and incorporation comes before capital is brought in.

This guide sets out how a foreign investor sets up a company in Nepal, from the legal framework to the practical sequence.

Quick answer

Foreign investment in Nepal is governed mainly by the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act (FITTA), 2075, read with the Companies Act, 2063. Most investors incorporate a private limited company. Approval from the Department of Industry, or the Investment Board Nepal for larger projects, comes before incorporation. Capital must enter through banking channels and be recorded at Nepal Rastra Bank.

The legal framework

FITTA 2075 sets out how foreign investment is approved, how profits are repatriated, and which sectors are restricted. The Companies Act, 2063 governs how the company itself is formed and run. Around these sit sector regulators, such as the Nepal Electricity Authority for energy, and the foreign exchange rules of Nepal Rastra Bank. None of this is unusual by regional standards, but it means the approvals are layered, and skipping a layer costs time.

Choosing the structure

Most foreign investors incorporate a private limited company. It offers limited liability, flexible governance and simpler reporting, which makes it the standard vehicle for a wholly owned subsidiary or a joint venture. A public limited company is possible but heavier, and is rarely the right choice at entry.

The process, step by step

  1. Confirm sector eligibility against Nepal's negative list.
  2. Obtain foreign investment approval from the Department of Industry, or the Investment Board Nepal above the applicable threshold.
  3. Clear the company name at the Office of the Company Registrar.
  4. Draft and notarise the memorandum and articles of association.
  5. Incorporate and obtain the certificate of incorporation.
  6. Register for PAN, and for VAT where applicable.
  7. Open a corporate bank account and bring the capital in through banking channels.
  8. Complete Nepal Rastra Bank reporting on the capital inflow.
  9. Obtain sector licences where required.

A worked example

A Southeast Asian group wants to build a mid-sized manufacturing plant in Nepal. Manufacturing is open to foreign investment, so the route is well trodden, but the project size brings it within a higher approval threshold. The group starts by confirming sector eligibility, then prepares a project report for approval, then incorporates the Nepali subsidiary, then remits capital through the bank and has it recorded. NEA and local approvals follow for utilities and land. Run in the right order, the file moves steadily. Run out of order, the group discovers that the capital it already sent cannot be recognised, and the whole sequence stalls.

Approvals and clearances

Depending on sector and size, approval may come from the Department of Industry, the Investment Board Nepal, or, for certain regulated activities, a sector regulator. Capital inflow and repatriation are handled under Nepal Rastra Bank's foreign exchange framework. The Nepal Electricity Authority, the Nepal Tourism Board and similar bodies impose their own licensing conditions.

What is changing

Compliance expectations are rising across the board, particularly around beneficial ownership disclosure and anti-money-laundering rules. Companies with foreign shareholding often carry additional audit and reporting duties. Engaging local counsel early, before the structure is fixed, tends to reduce delay more than any single filing.

Frequently asked questions

Does a foreign investor need approval before incorporating? Yes. Foreign investment approval comes before incorporation.

What is the minimum investment for a foreign investor? Nepal sets a general minimum, currently NPR 20 million per foreign investor, with sector-specific variations. Confirm the current figure before structuring.

Can a foreigner own 100% of a Nepali company? In sectors not on the negative list, generally yes.

How long does the whole process take? Typically several weeks to a couple of months, depending on the sector, the approvals involved and how quickly documents are legalised.

Can capital be repatriated? Yes, after tax clearance and Nepal Rastra Bank approval, provided the investment was properly documented.

Which structure is most common? A private limited company, whether wholly owned or a joint venture.

title: Key Corporate Law Reforms in Nepal: What Directors Need to Know
content:
Directors in Nepal often assume that their duties are settled, set out once in the Companies Act and unlikely to change. The reality is gentler and more demanding at the same time. The core duties are stable, but the way regulators and courts expect them to be applied keeps moving, particularly around disclosure and personal accountability. A board that ran cleanly five years ago can be quietly out of step today.

This guide explains what directors are expected to do, and where the scrutiny has shifted.

Quick answer

Directors of Nepali companies operate under the Companies Act, 2063, which codifies fiduciary duties to act in good faith, avoid conflicts of interest, and exercise the care of a reasonably prudent person. Around this, regulatory practice has tightened disclosure, related-party dealings and beneficial ownership reporting, and courts have shown a willingness to hold directors personally accountable in distress situations. Staying current is part of the job.

The Companies Act as the foundation

The Companies Act, 2063 remains the primary source of directors' duties. It requires directors to act honestly and in the company's interest, to avoid putting themselves in a position where duty and personal interest conflict, and to bring reasonable care and skill to their role. These duties are owed to the company itself, which matters when a director later tries to argue that a decision was good for shareholders or for a particular family.

Where scrutiny has increased

  • Timely and accurate financial reporting to shareholders and the Office of the Company Registrar.
  • Proper maintenance of statutory registers and minutes of board meetings.
  • Disclosure of transactions with related parties and connected persons.
  • Compliance with beneficial ownership reporting under anti-money-laundering rules.
  • Approval of significant asset transfers and major financing arrangements.

The common thread is transparency. Regulators increasingly treat the quality of a board's records as a measure of the board itself.

Conflicts of interest

A director with an interest in a transaction must disclose it and, in most cases, step back from the relevant resolution. Failing to do so can expose the director to personal liability and allow the transaction to be unwound at the company's instance. The practical habit that prevents most problems is a standing conflict-of-interest item at every board meeting, recorded in the minutes.

Insolvency and personal liability

Judicial trends have made directors personally accountable for trading while the company is insolvent and for preferences that disadvantage creditors. A board that suspects the company is in difficulty should take advice before continuing to trade, because the decision to keep going is itself a decision the law scrutinises.

A worked example

A family-owned company wants to lease premises owned by its managing director. Done properly, the director discloses the interest, takes no part in the vote, and the remaining directors approve the lease on documented market terms. The minutes record all of it. Done casually, with the same director voting, the lease can later be challenged, and the director can be called to account. The substance of the two situations is nearly identical. The difference is the paper trail, and that is exactly what regulators and courts look at.

Practical steps for the year ahead

  1. Schedule an annual governance review so duties and filings are checked, not assumed.
  2. Update the company's internal bylaws to reflect current practice.
  3. Verify that statutory filings and registers are current and complete.
  4. Put related-party and beneficial ownership disclosures on a standing agenda.
  5. Have external counsel audit board practices against current expectations.

Frequently asked questions

What are a director's basic duties in Nepal? To act in good faith in the company's interest, avoid conflicts of interest, and exercise reasonable care and diligence.

Can a director be personally liable? Yes. Personal liability can arise from undisclosed conflicts, trading while insolvent, and certain preferences to creditors.

What must be disclosed in a related-party transaction? The interest must be disclosed, and the director should abstain from the relevant resolution in most cases.

Are minutes and registers really that important? Yes. They are the evidence of how a board made its decisions, and regulators treat them as a measure of governance.

What is beneficial ownership reporting? A requirement to disclose the natural persons who ultimately own or control the company, under anti-money-laundering rules.

What should a board do when the company is in difficulty? Take advice early. The decision to keep trading can itself attract scrutiny.

title: Trademark Registration in Nepal: A Practical Guide for Businesses
content:
A brand is often worth more than the premises it is sold from, yet plenty of businesses in Nepal trade for years without ever registering their name. Nothing goes wrong until it does: a copycat opens nearby, a former partner launches under a similar mark, or an online listing uses your name to draw your customers. Registration is what turns a name you use into a right you can enforce.

This guide explains how trademark registration works in Nepal and why the timing of your filing matters.

Quick answer

Trademarks in Nepal are registered with the Department of Industry under the Patent, Design and Trademark Act, 2022. Registration grants a statutory monopoly over the mark and a clear basis to act against counterfeiters and copycats. The process runs from a preliminary search, through examination, to publication and registration. A registered mark is valid for seven years and can be renewed.

Where you file

The Department of Industry administers patents, industrial designs and trademarks from its office in Kathmandu. Because one office handles all three, the system is centralised, which makes the filing route predictable. The trade-off is that a busy office rewards a well-prepared application over a rushed one.

The registration process

  1. Preliminary search. Check for conflicting marks already on the register before you commit to a name or a filing.
  2. File the application. Include a representation of the mark and the applicant's details.
  3. Examination. The Department of Industry examines the mark for distinctiveness and conflicts.
  4. Publication. The mark is published, opening a window for opposition.
  5. Registration. If no opposition succeeds, the mark is registered.

Why distinctiveness matters

A mark must be capable of distinguishing your goods or services from those of others. Descriptive words, common surnames and generic terms are frequently rejected, unless they have acquired a distinct meaning through long use. A name that describes exactly what you sell is easy to market and hard to protect. A name that is distinctive may need a little more explanation, but it is the one that can be defended.

Duration and renewal

A registered trademark is initially valid for seven years and can be renewed for successive periods. Renewal is a simple filing, but missing the deadline can remove the mark from the register, and rebuilding protection after a lapse is far harder than keeping it alive.

A worked example

Two cafes open in the same district within a year of each other, both called something close to a well-known coffee brand. Neither registered. When the original brand owner enters Nepal, both are served notice. The owner who filed a trademark application early is in a strong position to oppose the copy or to license the mark. The owner who relied on the common law of passing off must prove reputation and confusion, which is slower and more expensive, and the outcome is less certain. The cost of the filing, paid early, is trivial next to the cost of the dispute.

Enforcing your rights

A registered proprietor can oppose conflicting applications, demand that infringing use stop, and pursue civil remedies or criminal action. An unregistered mark can only rely on passing off, which requires proving goodwill and misrepresentation and is both harder and costlier. Registration does not remove the need to police a mark, but it changes the odds decisively in your favour.

Frequently asked questions

How long does trademark registration take in Nepal? It varies with examination and any opposition, but the process is predictable once the application is filed. A search before filing avoids the most common delay.

How long is a trademark valid? Seven years initially, renewable for successive periods.

Can I register a descriptive name? Usually not, unless it has acquired a distinct meaning through use.

What can I do if someone copies my mark? If registered, you can oppose their application and act against their use. If unregistered, you depend on passing off, which is harder to prove.

Do I need the mark registered before I use it? You can use a mark before registering it, but you gain enforceable rights only on registration.

Does a foreign trademark cover me in Nepal? No. Protection is territorial, so a mark registered abroad does not protect you in Nepal.

title: Renewable Energy Projects in Nepal: Legal and Regulatory Overview
content:
Nepal's rivers have powered the country for generations, and they remain the centre of its energy ambitions. A hydropower project is also one of the most heavily regulated investments anyone can make here, not because the law is hostile, but because a river is a shared resource and a large dam touches land, forests, communities and the national grid at once. Developers who understand the licensing chain early move faster than those who learn it by trial.

This guide gives an overview of the legal and regulatory framework for renewable energy projects in Nepal, with a focus on hydropower.

Quick answer

Renewable energy projects in Nepal are governed mainly by the Electricity Act, 2049 and the Electricity Regulations, 2050, with larger priority projects falling under the Investment Board Act. A developer needs a survey licence, then a generation licence, plus environmental approval. Power is normally sold to the Nepal Electricity Authority under a power purchase agreement. Foreign investment adds approval and repatriation requirements.

The primary legislation

The Electricity Act, 2049 and the Electricity Regulations, 2050 govern the generation, transmission and distribution of electricity. The Investment Board Act applies to projects that fall within the national priority thresholds and are handled by the Investment Board Nepal. Alongside these sit environmental law, land and forest rules, and, for foreign investors, FITTA and Nepal Rastra Bank's foreign exchange framework.

Licensing requirements

A project typically needs these in sequence:

  • A survey licence to carry out studies and feasibility assessments.
  • An electricity generation licence once the survey and studies are complete.
  • Approval of an environmental impact assessment (EIA), or an initial environmental examination (IEE) for smaller projects.

Each stage depends on the one before it, which is why a project can be delayed substantially by an incomplete study or an environmental file that is submitted too early.

Power purchase agreements

The Nepal Electricity Authority is the principal off-taker. The terms of the power purchase agreement, including tariffs and take-or-pay obligations, are negotiated against the prevailing regulatory framework and often decide whether a project is bankable. Because the PPA sits at the centre of project revenue, its negotiation deserves as much care as the technical design.

Project finance

Lenders typically require a complete chain of land rights, generation and transmission licences, a signed PPA, and adequate insurance before they will commit. Foreign investors should confirm whether their project needs Investment Board Nepal approval or a sectoral licence. Most financing delays trace back to a gap in the licence chain rather than to the money itself.

Environmental and social compliance

Hydropower and renewable projects face close environmental and social scrutiny. Resettlement, forest clearance and river-flow obligations must be addressed in the EIA and monitored through the life of the project. These are not only legal requirements. They are also, increasingly, what a project's lenders and off-takers expect to see properly handled.

A worked example

A foreign developer identifies a run-of-river site and secures a survey licence. The feasibility study is thorough, and the land rights chain is assembled before the environmental file is finalised, so the generation licence and EIA approval are not held up by a missing link. The PPA is negotiated with a clear tariff and take-or-pay terms, and the lenders are satisfied. A second developer moves faster and applies for the generation licence before land rights are settled. The file stalls for months, the PPA window narrows, and the financing costs rise. The technical projects are similar. The disciplined sequence is what separates them.

Frequently asked questions

What licences does a hydropower project need? A survey licence, an electricity generation licence, and environmental approval, in sequence.

Who buys the electricity? The Nepal Electricity Authority is the principal off-taker, under a power purchase agreement.

Is environmental approval always required? Yes, in some form. Larger projects need a full EIA, while smaller projects may qualify for an IEE.

Do foreign investors need separate approval? Often yes, especially for larger projects under the Investment Board Nepal, and always under FITTA for the foreign investment itself.

What do lenders require? A complete land rights chain, the relevant licences, a signed PPA, and adequate insurance.

How long does licensing take? It varies widely with project size and the completeness of the studies and environmental file. The sequence, not the calendar, is the main variable.

title: Employment Law in Nepal: Employee Rights and Employer Obligations
content:
Hiring your first employee in Nepal feels simple until the paperwork arrives. The Labour Act sets minimum standards that apply whether or not an employer has thought about them, and the obligations mostly fall on the employer by default. A business that treats employment as a handshake tends to discover the rules only when a dispute or an inspection forces the question.

This guide explains the main employer obligations under the Labour Act, 2074, and how to stay compliant without overcomplicating the basics.

Quick answer

The Labour Act, 2074 governs employment in Nepal and applies to most private sector employers. It prescribes minimum standards for written contracts, working hours, leave, termination and social security. Employers must issue written contracts, keep proper records, contribute to the Social Security Fund, and follow the statutory procedure before terminating employment.

Written employment contracts

An employer must provide a written contract or appointment letter to every employee. The document should set out the nature of the work, the remuneration, the working hours, and the grounds and procedure for termination. A clear contract protects both sides, and it is the first thing a labour office will ask to see if there is a complaint.

Working hours and leave

The standard working week is limited to 48 hours, with overtime payable for additional work. Employees are entitled to annual leave, sick leave and public holidays, along with maternity and paternity leave as prescribed by the statute. These are minimums, not suggestions, and they cannot be traded away in a contract.

Termination and severance

Termination must follow the procedure in the Labour Act. An employee whose services are terminated, other than for misconduct, is entitled to notice or pay in lieu, and to gratuity and leave encashment where applicable. The procedural steps matter as much as the money: a termination that is fair in substance but wrong in process can still be found unlawful.

Social security

Registered employers must contribute to the Social Security Fund on behalf of their employees. Contributions cover medical, accident, dependency and pension benefits, and late or non-payment attracts penalties. Enrolling new staff promptly, rather than in a batch at year end, avoids both the penalty and the administrative scramble.

Practical compliance steps

  • Maintain attendance records, payroll documentation and statutory registers.
  • Issue written contracts and keep signed copies on file.
  • Enrol employees in the Social Security Fund on time.
  • Ensure workplace policies meet anti-discrimination and occupational safety obligations.
  • Follow the statutory process before any termination.

A worked example

A growing marketing firm hires eight staff in a year and, being busy, issues offer letters that omit the termination procedure and working hours. When one employee's performance fails to improve, the firm dismisses him with immediate effect. The dismissal is overturned as procedurally flawed, and the firm pays compensation it could have avoided. A one-page contract drafted at the start, with the statutory procedure spelled out, would have made the same decision defensible. The lesson is common to most labour disputes: the paperwork you disliked at the beginning is the paperwork that protects you at the end.

Frequently asked questions

Is a written contract required? Yes. Employers must provide a written contract or appointment letter to every employee.

What is the maximum working week? 48 hours, with overtime payable beyond that.

What is an employee entitled to on termination? Notice or pay in lieu, and gratuity and leave encashment where applicable, unless the termination is for misconduct.

Must employers contribute to the Social Security Fund? Yes. Registered employers must contribute on behalf of their employees.

What happens if contributions are late? Penalties apply, and the arrears remain payable.

Does the Labour Act apply to all employers? It applies to most private sector employers, with limited exceptions.

title: Divorce in Nepal: Process, Cost and Timeline Explained
content:
Deciding to end a marriage is rarely a single moment. For most people it follows a long period of trying to make things work, and by the time they speak to a lawyer they are carrying both the emotional weight of the decision and a set of practical fears about money, children and paperwork. The law in Nepal is clearer than many expect, but it moves along two very different tracks, and knowing which one you are on early makes the whole process easier to bear.

This guide explains both tracks, what each involves, and how to prepare, so you can make decisions calmly rather than under pressure.

Quick answer

There are two routes to divorce in Nepal. A mutual consent divorce, under Section 93 of the Muluki Civil Code, 2074, is when both spouses agree to end the marriage and settle the terms. A contested divorce, based on a recognised ground, is when one spouse does not agree or the terms cannot be settled. Mutual cases are faster and cheaper. Contested cases take longer, because the court must decide custody, maintenance and property along the way.

The law behind it

Divorce in Nepal is governed by Chapter 3 of the National Civil Code, 2074 (the Muluki Civil Code), and by the National Civil Procedure Code for the process itself. The case is filed in the Family Court, or in the District Court with jurisdiction over the respondent's locality. Because the route and the outcome both turn on the facts, the advice worth having is advice about your facts, not about divorce in the abstract.

Grounds for divorce

Under Section 94, either spouse may petition on grounds such as adultery, desertion, physical or mental cruelty, or having lived apart for three or more consecutive years. Section 95 gives a wife additional grounds, including polygamy by the husband and marital rape. If your situation does not fall neatly into one of these, a mutual consent filing may be the more honest route.

How a mutual consent divorce works

Both spouses file a joint petition and agree the terms. Where children, maintenance or property are involved, those terms should be written into the petition so they are settled, not left for a later dispute. In practice this is the route most couples choose when the relationship has ended without open conflict, because it closes the matter in weeks rather than years. The court can decree the divorce after the prescribed period, which is designed to give both parties time to reconsider.

How a contested divorce works

When only one spouse wants the divorce, or the two cannot agree, the petition must state a recognised ground and the case proceeds through hearings, evidence and, frequently, reconciliation attempts. The court will decide custody, maintenance and how jointly acquired property is divided. Because these decisions are discretionary, the quality of the evidence prepared at the start often decides the outcome more than anything said in the final hearing.

How long it takes

Route Typical timeframe
Mutual consent A few weeks to two to three months after the court accepts the petition
Contested, no major disputes Around one to two years from filing
Contested with custody or property disputes Longer still, and longer again if the respondent cannot be traced

These are realistic ranges, not promises. Court load and the cooperation of both parties move the timeline more than anything else.

Documents you will normally need

  • Citizenship certificates of both spouses
  • The marriage registration certificate, or court marriage certificate
  • Birth certificates for any children
  • Evidence supporting any claim over property or maintenance
  • A properly authenticated power of attorney if a spouse lives abroad

What it costs

The court fee on a divorce plaint in a district court is modest, often a few hundred rupees. The larger cost is professional fees, which depend on whether the matter is mutual or contested and how much negotiation and hearing time it needs. A mutual file can usually be handled on a fixed fee. A contested matter with property and custody issues is typically billed on milestones. Whichever applies, ask for a written fee structure before you engage anyone.

A worked example

A couple who married in Kathmandu and now live in Australia want to divorce by agreement, but neither can easily return. They sign a power of attorney before a notary in Australia, have it attested by the Nepali embassy, and their Nepali lawyer files a mutual consent petition in Kathmandu. The terms on their apartment and on child maintenance are set out in the petition, so there is nothing left to argue about later. The matter is done without either of them flying home. Had one of them opposed the divorce, the same facts would have taken a much longer and more expensive route, and at least one appearance would likely have been required.

Divorce when a spouse lives abroad

Nepali couples living overseas can often complete a mutual consent divorce by power of attorney, avoiding a return to Nepal. Contested cases are harder to run remotely and usually need at least one appearance by the petitioner, or cross-examination of a witness.

Custody, maintenance and property

The court decides custody in the interest of the child, weighing the child's welfare and age against the care each parent can provide. Maintenance reflects the needs of the dependent spouse and children and the ability of the person paying. Property acquired during the marriage through joint effort is generally divided, while ancestral and individually owned property is treated separately. These questions are where most of the emotion in a case sits, and where calm, early advice pays off most.

Practical steps to take

  1. Speak to a family lawyer before filing, so the right route and grounds are chosen.
  2. Gather the documents above, including the original marriage certificate.
  3. If the divorce is mutual, put the terms on custody, maintenance and property in writing first.
  4. File with the correct court and attend the required hearings.
  5. After the decree, update your records and register any new marriage.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a divorce take in Nepal? A mutual consent divorce is typically finalised within a few weeks to two to three months once the court accepts the petition. A contested divorce generally takes one to two years, and longer where custody or property is disputed.

Can I divorce without going to court? No. Even a mutual consent divorce requires a court decree. The agreement shapes the case, but the court issues the order.

Can we divorce in Nepal if we married abroad? Often yes, depending on your citizenship and where the respondent lives. A Nepali couple who married abroad can generally proceed in Nepal, and the marriage may need to be registered here first.

Do I need my spouse's agreement to divorce? No. A contested divorce is available on a recognised ground without the other spouse's consent, though it takes longer.

What happens to property on divorce? Property acquired during the marriage through joint effort is generally divided. Ancestral and individually owned property is treated separately.

Can a spouse abroad be divorced without returning? In mutual cases, usually yes, through an authenticated power of attorney. Contested cases often require an appearance.

title: How to Register an NGO in Nepal: A Step-by-Step Guide
content:
People who set out to do good in Nepal often hit a wall they did not expect, and it is rarely about the cause. It is about paperwork. The registration route for a non-profit depends on whom you intend to serve and where your funding comes from, and choosing the wrong route at the start can stall an organisation before it has done any work at all.

This guide explains the two main routes for non-profits in Nepal, the third path for international organisations, and how to keep a registration in good standing once it is granted.

Quick answer

There are two domestic routes and one international one. A local non-profit registers with the District Administration Office (DAO) if it will work within Nepal under domestic funding. An organisation that operates nationally or receives foreign funding affiliates with the Social Welfare Council (SWC) as well. An International NGO (INGO) enters Nepal under the Social Welfare Act and an agreement with the SWC, and must work through local partners rather than operating directly in the community.

NGO and INGO: what the words mean in practice

In everyday use, an NGO is a domestic non-profit registered with the DAO and affiliated with the Social Welfare Council. An INGO is a foreign non-profit that enters Nepal under the Social Welfare Act and an agreement with the SWC. The distinction matters because an INGO cannot simply run its own projects here. It channels its work through local NGO partners, and its approval process is more regulated.

Step 1: Form the founding committee

You need a group of founding members, usually five or more Nepali citizens, who will form the general assembly and elect an executive committee. Their citizenship certificates, and in most cases passports, are required. Getting the founding group right at this stage saves redoing the documents later.

Step 2: Draft the constitution

The constitution is the heart of the application. It should set out the organisation's name, objectives, area of operation, membership, the composition and tenure of the executive committee, how decisions are taken, and how funds are managed. Supporting documents include the minutes of the formation meeting, the election of office bearers, and the PAN application of the institution. A constitution that is vague about objectives or about how funds are controlled is the most common reason a file is sent back.

Step 3: Register at the District Administration Office

The complete file goes to the DAO of the district where the organisation is based. The DAO reviews the constitution and documents and, once satisfied, issues the registration. This registration gives the organisation legal personality, which it needs before it can open a bank account or sign agreements in its own name.

Step 4: Affiliate with the Social Welfare Council

A registered NGO that intends to receive foreign funding, or to operate beyond the local level, typically registers with and seeks affiliation from the Social Welfare Council. Affiliation is what unlocks access to funding and to formal national recognition. The SWC reviews the constitution, the DAO registration and the organisation's work plan.

Step 5: Bank account and PAN

With the DAO registration and, where applicable, SWC affiliation in hand, the organisation can open a bank account in its own name and complete its tax registration to receive a PAN. These are the prerequisites for receiving funding, issuing receipts and employing staff.

A worked example

A group in Lalitpur wants to run a literacy programme funded entirely by local donors. It follows the DAO route, publishes a clear constitution, and keeps its work within the district. A second group wants to run the same programme but with a European foundation as its funder. That funding brings the Social Welfare Council into the picture, and with it a stricter review of the constitution and work plan. Had the second group registered only with the DAO and then accepted foreign funding, it would have had to pause and restructure mid-programme. Deciding at the outset which route fits your funding is the single most useful early choice.

Ongoing compliance

A non-profit must file annual reports and financial statements with the DAO and, where affiliated, with the Social Welfare Council to keep its registration current. Falling behind on reporting is the most common reason an organisation's status lapses and funding is interrupted. Renewal and reporting dates vary by office, so a compliance calendar from day one is worth the small effort.

Frequently asked questions

How many founding members are needed? Usually five or more Nepali citizens, who form the general assembly and elect the executive committee.

Do I need Social Welfare Council affiliation? If you intend to receive foreign funding or operate beyond the local level, yes. It is central to accessing funding and national recognition.

What is the difference between an NGO and an INGO? An NGO is a domestic non-profit registered with the DAO. An INGO is a foreign non-profit entering Nepal under the Social Welfare Act and working through local partners.

Can an INGO operate directly in Nepal? Generally it must work through local NGO partners rather than operating directly in the community.

Does an NGO need a PAN? Yes. A PAN is required for receiving funding, issuing receipts and employing staff.

What happens if annual reports are missed? The registration and affiliation can lapse, which interrupts funding. Reporting discipline keeps the organisation in good standing.

title: NRN Investment in Nepal: How Non-Resident Nepalis Can Invest
content:
For many non-resident Nepalis, investing back home is both a financial decision and an emotional one. There is a family business to support, or a plot of land to develop, or simply a wish to keep a stake in the country you grew up in. The good news is that NRNs are welcome to invest, and the framework exists. The part that trips people up is the same one that catches every foreign investor: the approvals come before the money, not after.

This guide explains how NRN investment works in Nepal, where the diaspora route differs, and what to get right so your capital is not stranded.

Quick answer

Non-resident Nepalis can invest in Nepal under the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act (FITTA), which treats NRNs as permitted foreign investors. The usual approvals apply: sector eligibility, approval from the Department of Industry, and registration with the Office of the Company Registrar. In some cases the NRN route carries a lower entry threshold than the general foreign investment minimum, so it is worth confirming the current policy before you structure anything.

Is the NRN route different?

NRNs are foreign investors under FITTA, so the framework is familiar. What differs is treatment. Certain concessions are available to the diaspora, and some technology-based or smaller investments can qualify for a lower threshold than the general minimum. These are policy details that change, which is exactly why they should be checked at the time you invest rather than assumed from something read a year ago.

Ways an NRN can invest

  • A new company in an eligible sector, usually a private limited company with the NRN as shareholder. This is the most common route.
  • Investment in an existing company, by subscribing to new shares, subject to sector limits and the company's approval.
  • Listed securities, meaning portfolio investment in shares on the Nepal Stock Exchange, which follows separate rules for non-residents.
  • A branch or joint venture, where the NRN invests alongside Nepali or other partners.

Minimum investment and sector eligibility

The general minimum foreign investment threshold in Nepal is currently NPR 20 million, and individual sectors carry their own limits or are reserved for Nepali citizens. Energy, tourism, IT and manufacturing are broadly open. Some service and retail activities are reserved. Technology-based investments in certain cases benefit from a lower or waived threshold. Confirm sector eligibility before committing money, because a structure that cannot be approved wastes both the filing cost and months of time.

The process, step by step

  1. Confirm sector eligibility and the minimum investment that applies to an NRN.
  2. Submit the foreign investment application to the Department of Industry and obtain approval.
  3. Reserve the company name and prepare the memorandum and articles of association.
  4. Incorporate at the Office of the Company Registrar and obtain the certificate.
  5. Register for PAN and, where applicable, VAT.
  6. Open a corporate bank account and route the investment through authorised banking channels.

Do you need to be in Nepal?

Much of the process can be handled remotely. A shareholder resolution and a power of attorney can be notarised abroad and authenticated, and a local representative can complete the filings. In practice, being available for one visit at the key banking stage smooths things out, but it is not always essential. Our guide to setting up a company in Nepal walks through the incorporation step by step.

A worked example

An NRN in the United States wants to buy 30% of an existing Nepali software company. Because the sector is open and the investment meets the threshold, the route is manageable. He starts by confirming eligibility, then files for foreign investment approval, then subscribes to new shares. The capital enters through his bank, not hand to hand, and is recorded at the central bank. Two years later, when he wants to repatriate a dividend, the paper trail from that original transfer is what makes the remittance smooth. An NRN who wires money informally in year one often finds the same funds impossible to send back in year three.

Repatriation of profits and capital

Profits, dividends and, on winding up, capital can be repatriated subject to Nepal Rastra Bank approval and the company's tax obligations. The key is documentation: funds should enter through the banking system and the equity should be reflected in the company's records. Keep your NRN status and papers current, because repatriation depends on being able to show exactly where the money came from.

Common pitfalls

  • Committing to a sector that is closed to foreign investment.
  • Bringing funds in informally, which then blocks repatriation.
  • Skipping notarisation and authentication, causing delays at the registrar or the bank.
  • Confusing company registration with foreign investment approval, when both are required.

Frequently asked questions

Can an NRN own 100% of a Nepali company? In sectors not on the negative list, generally yes.

Is the minimum investment lower for NRNs? Sometimes, depending on the sector and the type of investment. Confirm the current policy before structuring.

Can an NRN invest while living abroad? Yes, largely. Notarised and authenticated documents and a local representative allow most of the process to be handled remotely.

Can an NRN repatriate profits? Yes, after tax clearance and Nepal Rastra Bank approval, provided the original investment was documented.

Does an NRN need foreign investment approval? Yes. NRNs are treated as foreign investors under FITTA and require approval.

Can an NRN buy land in Nepal? An NRN who holds Nepali citizenship generally can. An NRN who has taken foreign citizenship faces the same property restrictions as other foreign nationals. See our guide on foreigners buying property.
